claims.text: In titanium-containing high-entropy alloy superconductors with heavy transition metals, superconducting Tc is governed by local lattice distortions.
Atomic-size and bonding mismatches induce the relevant local lattice distortions.
Local lattice distortions modulate electron–phonon coupling strength.
Controlled annealing can reduce local chemical disorder and promote more uniform short-range order without phase separation.
Reducing local chemical disorder enhances electron coherence.
Reducing local chemical disorder raises Tc relative to the as-cast state.
The proposed starting material is a single-phase, fully random solid solution containing at least five elements, including titanium and one or more heavy transition metals.
Every constituent must remain at or above 5 atomic percent.
The alloy must remain a single-phase solid solution so that the effects of local distortion and chemical order can be isolated.
Strong scattering associated with lattice distortions in the fully disordered state suppresses electron pairing.
Annealing homogenizes local bond lengths.
Homogenizing local bond lengths strengthens electron–phonon coupling.
The annealed sample will have a higher Tc than the identically composed as-cast sample.
The annealed sample will show sharper superconducting transitions in resistivity and magnetic susceptibility.
Sharper resistive and susceptibility transitions indicate enhanced electron coherence.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to multiphase or partially ordered alloys.
The magnitude of the Tc response depends on elemental selection, atomic-size mismatch, and annealing details.
Other scattering mechanisms may influence superconducting behavior.
XRD and TEM can verify the intended change in short-range order and exclusion of secondary phases.
Failure of annealing to produce a statistically significant Tc increase or sharper transition relative to the as-cast control would falsify the stated hypothesis.
